dialogue.shona: Ndiri kunwa mushonga mushure mekudya sezvandakaudzwa nachiremba.
dialogue.english: I am taking medicine after eating, just as I was told by the doctor.
dialogue.literal_gloss: Ndiri [ndiri] • kunwa [to / at nwa] • mushonga [in / singular shonga] • mushure [in / singular shure] • mekudya [mekudya] • sezvandakaudzwa [sezvandakaudzwa] • nachiremba [nachiremba]

grammar_notes.title: Actions Happening Right Now: The '-ri ku-' Progressive
grammar_notes.content: To describe an action that is happening right now ('I am doing', 'it is raining', 'they are walking'), Shona uses the helper verb '-ri' ('am/is/are') followed by 'ku-' ('to') and the action verb. For people, the forms are 'ndiri ku-' (I am), 'uri ku-' (you are), 'ari ku-' (he/she is), 'tiri ku-' (we are), and 'vari ku-' (they are). In fast speech or writing, the two words are sometimes joined together (e.g., 'ndiri kuenda' or 'ndirikuenda').
grammar_notes.rule: [Subject + -ri] + ku-[verb] -> Ndiri kuverenga (I am reading) | Vari kufamba (They are walking) | Mvura iri kunaya (It is raining)

grammar_notes.title: How Shona Sentences Fit Together (Subject + Tense + Verb)
grammar_notes.content: In 'Ndiri kunwa mushonga mushure mekudya sezvandakaudzwa nachiremba.', notice how a single Shona verb word packs together who is doing the action (the subject prefix), when it happens (the tense marker), and the action itself (the verb stem). Once you recognize the building blocks at the start of the verb—like 'ndi-' (I), 'u-' (you), 'ti-' (we), or 'va-' (they)—you can immediately spot the subject even when no separate pronoun word is used!
grammar_notes.rule: [Who (Subject Prefix)] + [When (Tense Marker)] + [Action (Verb Root)] -> e.g., ti- (we) + -cha- (will) + -svika (arrive) = tichasvika

grammar_notes.title: Describing Nouns: Word Order in Shona
grammar_notes.content: In English, descriptive words like adjectives, possessives ('my', 'our'), demonstratives ('this', 'that'), and numbers come BEFORE the noun ('this big house', 'my two books'). In Shona, the noun always comes FIRST, and all descriptive words follow right after it! For example: 'nyama iyi' ('this meat'), 'mwana uyu' ('this child'), 'goho guru' ('a big harvest'), and 'makomo marefu' ('tall mountains').
grammar_notes.rule: Noun FIRST + Descriptor SECOND -> mota iyi (this car), mabhuku edu (our books), makomo marefu (tall mountains)

cultural_notes.title: Following the Doctor's Advice ('Chiremba') & Taking Medicine After Meals
cultural_notes.content: Notice two natural Shona expressions here: 'kunwa mushonga' (literally 'to drink medicine', used for both liquid medicine and swallowing tablets) and 'chiremba' (the respected traditional and modern title for a qualified medical doctor).

active_exercises.prompt: How do you politely ask someone to speak softly ('taura zvinyoronyoro')?
In 'Uya kuno undibatsire', what does the prefix '-ndi-' inside 'undibatsire' mean?
active_exercises.explanation: The object prefix '-ndi-' always means 'me', placed directly before the verb stem '-batsira' (help).

active_exercises.prompt: What does 'parutivi pemugwagwa' mean in 'Rori yakamira parutivi pemugwagwa'?
options: In the middle of the intersection
Beside the road / on the side of the road
active_exercises.correct_answer: Beside the road / on the side of the road
active_exercises.explanation: 'Parutivi pe-' means 'beside / at the side of', and 'mugwagwa' is 'road'.
